frase_gancho.texto: Twenty-five pieces of jade to give the night a face.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the night we move on to diplomacy. Look for a small, honey-colored slab where two figures from different peoples look each other in the face.

guion_corto.texto: This mask, about twenty-eight centimeters tall, is made of twenty-five plates of green jadeite, polished and assembled like a mosaic. The eyes and teeth are made of shell. It represents the Zapotec Bat god, lord of the night, of caves, and of the underworld. It has large, upright ears, a leaf-shaped nose, and feline fangs, and three dangling tabs hang from the chin. For the Zapotecs, caves were the womb of the earth: the place of the dead, but also the source of water and the place where maize seed was kept. That is why this god blends darkness with life. It comes from Monte Albán and is about two thousand years old.

guion_largo.texto:
In the Zapotec world, the night had a face, and it was this one. The bat was the master of caves, and caves were the door to the other world. But a cave is also a womb: water springs from it, and maize seed was kept there so it could germinate in the darkness. You have already seen how Teotihuacán built its great pyramid over a cave. Here the idea reappears, with wings.

This mask is a jade puzzle. Each of the twenty-five plates was cut and polished until it was smooth as a mirror, and then fitted together with the others. Jade was no ordinary jewel: for the peoples of Mesoamerica it was solidified water, the breath of life, the color of everything that grows. It is believed to have come from the Motagua Valley, in Guatemala, hundreds of kilometers from Monte Albán, and those distances are thought to have been covered on foot.

Look at the details of the animal. The large, upright ears have perforations for hanging ear ornaments, like those worn by nobles. The nose is leaf-shaped, like that of many bats that live in the region, and the jaws show feline fangs: a blend of creatures that inspires both fear and respect. The eyes and teeth are made of sea shell, which also came from far away, from the coasts. Every material in this mask is a story of trade.

What was it for? We do not know for certain. It is thought to have been a ritual object, perhaps a chest ornament for a ruler or an insignia for ceremonies; the three dangling tabs suggest a pectoral. What we do know is that it was an object of enormous value and that the bat, for the Zapotecs, was not a creature of bad luck.

In fact, in Mesoamerica the bat had a long career. The Maya imagined the underworld, Xibalbá, with a house full of bats that tested the heroes in the Popol Vuh, their sacred book, and a giant bat, Camazotz, cuts off the head of one of the twins. So this god is not a local oddity: it is part of a shared way of imagining the underground world.

Now notice the balance of the mask. It is an imposing face, yet it was made with an almost delicate care and symmetry. Whoever carved it wanted darkness to look beautiful. That is one of the keys of this hall: the Zapotecs did not hide death; they dressed it in jade.

There is a curious fact they might have appreciated. Long-nosed bats pollinate agaves, and in Oaxaca agaves are the basis of mezcal and, elsewhere, of pulque. In other words, without bats certain drinks of today would not exist. The Zapotecs did not explain it that way, but they knew that this animal of the night had something to do with what grows.

And when you step out of the darkness of this piece, remember the tomb you will see soon: that whole underground world, with its murals and its offerings, was the realm of the bat. A realm that inspired fear, but also promised that food would once again come out of the earth.

texto: Count the jade plates that make up the mask
Look for the large ears and the leaf-shaped nose
Notice the shell eyes and teeth

texto.Material: Mosaic of burnished jade (jadeite) with shell eyes and teeth and three slate pendants

texto.pregunta: Myth: For the ancient peoples of Mexico, the bat was only a symbol of evil.
texto.respuesta: Reality: For the Zapotecs it was tied to the night and death, but also to caves, water, and the maize seed: it was a god of darkness that promised life.
